translations.title: Canto XXXVI: Pastime
translations.text:
When I was a boy, I came
to study under the Muses.
One of them took me by the hand
and led me around that day
to see her workshop.

She showed me, one by one,
the tools of the art
and the different work
each one performs
in prose and verse.

I looked at her and said,
“Muse, what of the file?”
“The file wore out,” the goddess replied.
“We no longer use it.”

“But we must make another,” I said,
“since it is so necessary.”
“That is true,” she answered,
“but there is no time.”
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: I Have Always Loved This Hill...
translations.text:
I have always loved this hill
and the hedge that prevents me from seeing
beyond the horizon.

Looking far off into boundless spaces,
superhuman silences and their profound stillness,
I find myself with my thoughts,
and my heart is not afraid.

I hear the wind whistling over the fields,
and amid the infinite silence I sound out my voice:
eternity overcomes me, the dead seasons,
present reality and all its sounds.

Thus my thought drowns in this immensity,
and I am sweetly shipwrecked in this sea.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Infinite
translations.text:
This lonely hill has always been dear to me,
and this barrier, which shuts the farthest horizon
from sight on this side.

But seated here, gazing beyond it,
my mind imagines endless spaces,
superhuman silences and deepest stillness,
so deeply that my heart almost takes fright.

And as I hear the wind rustle among the plants,
I compare that infinite silence with this voice;
I remember eternity,
the dead seasons, and the present one,
alive with its sound.

Thus my thought sinks into this immensity,
and shipwreck in this sea is sweet to me.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Canto XXVIII: To Himself
translations.text:
You will rest forever,
weary heart! The illusion
I imagined eternal has died. It has died.
And I see that within me,
along with hope, even longing has died
for flattering dreams.

Rest forever;
your beating has gone on long enough.
Nothing is worthy of your pulse;
nor does the earth deserve a sigh.
Life is only striving and weariness,
and the world is mud.

Be still, and despair
for the last time: Fate granted our kind
only death. So, in your pride,
despise your life and Nature,
and the harsh power
that secretly rules
over universal ruin,
and the infinite vanity of all things.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Canto XIV: To the Moon
translations.text:
O gracious moon, I remember well
how a year ago I came in anguish
to gaze at you from this hill;
and you rose above that grove
as you do now, lighting everything.

But your face appeared to my eyes
trembling and blurred by the tears
that filled them, for my life was sorrowful.
It still is, and does not change,
O my beloved moon.

Yet I still take pleasure
in remembering and reliving the time
of my sorrow. How happy it is,
in youth, when hope stretches so far
and memory is still brief,
to recall things past,
even sad things, even when our troubles last!
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Here, Wandering About the Threshold...
translations.text:
Here, wandering about the threshold,
I call in vain upon rain and storm
to keep her in my home.

The hurricane roared in the forest
and thunder rumbled among the clouds
before dawn lit the sky.

O beloved clouds, sky, earth, plants!
My love is leaving: have pity, if pity
exists in this world for a sorrowful lover.

Awake, whirlwind, and try now,
O storm, to enfold me until the sun
renews the day in another land!

The sky clears; the wind falls still;
leaves and grass sleep, and the cruel sun,
dazzling me, fills my eyes with tears.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Canto XLI: From the Greek of Simonides
translations.text:
That human things last but a little while
is a very true saying,
says the old man of Chios,
for men and leaves
have the same nature.

But very few hear these words.
All give shelter
to restless hope,
born in youthful hearts.

While the flowers of our tender years
are still red, the proud soul
nourishes a hundred sweet thoughts in vain.
It expects neither death nor old age;
no sickness troubles the healthy man.

But foolish is he who fails to see
how quickly youth takes flight,
and how close the grave
stands to the cradle.

You, whose foot will soon step
upon the fateful road
to Pluto's realm,
entrust your brief life
to present joys.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Canto XXXVII: Fragment
translations.text:
ALCETA

Listen, Meliso: I must tell you a dream
I had last night, which comes back to me
as I look at the moon. I was standing
at the window overlooking the meadow,
gazing upward, when suddenly
the moon broke loose. It seemed to me
that the closer it came as it fell,
the larger it grew, until at last
it struck the middle of the meadow.
It was as large as a pitcher and spewed
a mist of sparks, hissing
like a burning coal plunged into water
and extinguished. In this way,
as I said, the moon went dark
little by little upon the field,
and the grass smoked around it.
Then I saw that in the sky remained
a glimmer, a trace, or perhaps a hollow
where it had been torn away.
I froze with terror, and still tremble.

MELISO

And well you should be afraid, for the moon
could easily have fallen in your field.

ALCETA

Who knows? Do we not see stars fall
in summer?

MELISO

There are so many stars
that it matters little if one or another falls,
with a thousand still remaining. But the moon
is alone in the sky, and no one has ever
seen it fall except in dreams.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: At Sunset, the Merry Girl...
translations.text:
At sunset, the merry girl
returns from the countryside
with her bundle of grass and flowering branch,
where violet and rose shine side by side.
Innocently she prepares it
to adorn her breast and hair
with joy when the festival comes.

Beside her neighbor,
an old woman sits spinning at her door,
her face turned toward the setting sun.
Her thoughts return to a far-off season
when, still a fresh young maiden,
she danced at the week's end
with the friends of her fairest years.

The air grows dark,
the horizons take on blue,
and shadows descend from the mountains
as the pale moon appears.
The village tower announces the festival,
and its cheerful chimes descend
to comfort every heart.

In the square a lively band of boys,
shouting and leaping here and there,
raises a joyful, stirring din,
while the farmer comes home whistling
and, seated at his table,
delights in the rest ahead.

When silence deepens with the shadows
and every light dies out,
I hear the hammer striking steadily
in the workshop, where the craftsman strives
to finish his task
before morning breaks.

This is the loveliest
and the last day of the week.
Tomorrow boredom and sorrow will return,
and everyone will go back
to customary work.

O charming boy!
Your sweet, blossoming age
is like a day full of joy,
a clear and peaceful day
before the festival of your life.
Enjoy it, then, enjoy it! This season
of flowers is gentle.
I will say no more; but do not weep
if the festival you long for is delayed.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: And God Made Me a Woman
translations.text:
And God made me a woman,
with long hair,
a woman's eyes, nose, and mouth.

With curves
and folds
and gentle hollows,
God hollowed me out inside,
made me a workshop
for human beings.

God delicately wove my nerves
and carefully balanced
the measure of my hormones.
God made my blood
and filled me with it
so it would flow
throughout my body;
thus were born
ideas,
dreams,
instinct.

God created it all gently,
with hammer blows of breath
and drill strokes of love,
the thousand and one things
that make me a woman every day,
for which I rise with pride
every morning
and bless my sex.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.
